title: DMS/NIGMS 2: Integrated Analysis of Fusion Protein Conformational Changes for Virus Entry
text:
The modeling platforms will be unique to study large-scale protein conformational changes by bridging 
multiple spatial and temporal scales involved in the virus fusion process. The machine learning facilitated 
enhanced sampling schemes, molecular and membrane models are generalizable, and should be broadly 
applicable for the study of many viruses and pathogens, and other processes involving protein 
conformational changes including endocytosis, exocytosis and sperm-egg fertilization.

title: Reprogramming of creatine metabolism in breast cancer metastasis
text:
The proposed research will shed light on how reprogramming of the creatine metabolic pathway participates in
breast cancer metastasis and help us to better understand key enzymes in creatine metabolism of breast
cancer. Creatine metabolism holds promise as prognostic indicator and potential therapeutic target for
metastatic breast cancer. We will develop integrated highly multiplexed mass spectrometry imaging and
immunohistochemistry approaches to detect creatine metabolic enzymes and creatine metabolites in breast
cancer specimens for future use in pathology workflows.

title: Neurogenetics of Vision Core
text: Imaging technologies such as confocal microscopy, multiphoton microscopy as well as optical coherence tomography and adaptive optics have transformed the ability of scientists to observe structural and functional changes in the visual system, in vivo and ex vivo, in both health and disease. The overarching goal of the imaging core is to transform the ability of vision scientists to use these critical technologies by providing access to and training on the newest imaging modalities, and transferring novel approaches between groups to facilitate innovation in research and collaboration across vision research disciplines. This goal will be achieved through supporting (1) access to new confocal and OCT/in vivo fluorescence microscopes as well as custom adaptive optics imaging ophthalmoscopes that will be made available through the Ophthalmology Department, (2) access to advanced imaging modalities available through various Stanford Microscopy Facilities, and (3) development, application and dissemination of customized in vivo imaging approaches and systems developed by investigators in the vision research center.

title: Pediatric Chronic Headache and COVID-19: Use of Machine Learning and Biobehavioral Analysis to Classify Headache Mechanism and Optimize Treatment Course.
text:
Chronic pain experienced by children has the potential to persist into adulthood and drive drug
addiction, mental health problems and suicidal behavior. The level of pain reported by children
who experience headache is immense and likely poorly estimated based on lowered ability of
children to articulate symptoms, potential malingering or underreporting of pain symptoms, and
extensive variability in physical growth and brain development. Headache is a frequently
reported and poorly understood primary and secondary disorder in pediatric subjects that shows
a sex-based effect. The variable presentation of headache underscores the potential for distinct
mechanisms of headache presentation, thus placing emphasis on tailored treatment options. In
the proposed research program, we investigate three phenotypically distinct forms of headache
in youth to understand the physiological mechanisms that govern their phenotypic presentation.
Taking advantage of a highly multidisciplinary and specialized research team in headache
research and clinical care, findings will greatly inform the diagnosis and treatment of childhood
headache and reduce future pain-related dependencies on healthcare resources.

title: Chemical proteomic investigation of lipid kinase specificity and druggability
text:
Diacylglycerol kinases (DGKs) are critical regulators of lipid signaling in mammalian biology and have remained
elusive drug targets. We propose the use of functional proteomics/metabolomics to address fundamental
questions regarding DGK ligand binding, diacylglycerol fatty acyl specificity, and druggability in T cells. The
overall impact of our findings is to enable new biological discoveries to broadly impact drug discovery of the DGK
superfamily.

title: Integrating deep learning, magnetic resonance imaging and genomics to study myocardial fibrosis
text:
Myocardial fibrosis is a common feature of multiple cardiovascular diseases and is a hallmark of cardiovascular
aging. The emergence of large biorepositories, such as the UK Biobank, with cardiac magnetic resonance
imaging (MRI) and whole genome sequence data in 100,000 participants, combined with the advent of machine
learning tools capable of generating imaging-based phenotypes at scale, offers a unique opportunity to study
myocardial fibrosis. This proposal leverages cardiac T1 mapping, a validated MRI tool for myocardial fibrosis
quantification, to advance our understanding of the genetic and non-genetic factors influencing myocardial
fibrosis, thus, enabling the development of prevention and therapeutic strategies aimed at mitigating myocardial
fibrosis and its associated morbidity.

title: Gene Editing and Virus Production Module
text: Resource/Service Core: Gene Editing and Virus Production Module Abstract The Gene Editing and Virus Production (GEVP) Module will provide access to state-of-the-art genome editing technologies and generate DNA/RNA constructs for use in mammalian cultures/systems in vision research. This Module will also purify and concentrate both lentivirus and adeno-associated virus (AAV) for subsequent use in immortalized, primary cultures (maintained by individual investigators and the Stem Cell, Organoid and Cell Phenotyping Module) and in animals in vivo. The specific services provided within the GEVP Module are; 1) CRISPR guide-RNA to perform DNA editing or epigenetic modifications, 2) site-directed mutagenesis for generating point mutations, insertions, or deletion variants, 3) shRNA plasmid generation for knockdown/out experiments, 4) full sequencing of generated constructs, extensive documentation, and maintenance of DNA stocks for future use, 5) small to large scale endotoxin free plasmid purification for downstream applications, thorough confirmation of produced constructs at the transcript, protein, and subcellular level, consultation for optimal promoters and serotypes, and 6) generation of high-purity viruses for use in vitro or in vivo. Overall, the GEVP Module will provide access to leading-edge genome editing technologies, support a range of DNA/RNA and viral technologies, and provide the assistance and expertise required to test unique hypotheses posited by vision scientists at UTSW and neighboring institutions.

title: Endothelial Cell Health Across the Spectrum of Cardiometabolic Disease
text:
(Public Health Relevance)
Given the rising burden of obesity, diabetes, and heart disease in the community, new approaches are needed
to maintain blood vessel health from the impact of cardiometabolic traits. The proposed research investigates
the impact of cardiometabolic diseases on health of the blood vessel lining cells, endothelial cells, by
measuring stress markers and gene expression pathways. Our results will clarify how cardiometabolic
diseases result in different patterns of endothelial cell gene expression and may identify novel molecular
underpinnings of cardiovascular risk that will have important preventive and therapeutic implications.

title: Project 2: Local and global epigenome regulation of senescence and aging
text: Studies in animal models reveal that genetic differences and somatic mutations underlie longevity, but that non-genetic contributions play a major role. Numerous observations, including from this PPG point to epigenetic alterations in chromatin as having a crucial role both in senescence and in aging. However, key questions remain, in particular, what are the driving epigenetic mechanisms that underlie cellular phenotypes that characterize senescence and aging? Our hypothesis is that normal chromatin processes include a drive toward stability or homeostasis of the epigenome, a process our PPG coined as “chromostasis”, however, chromostatic maintenance is imperfect and thus during aging leads to tissue deterioration and disease. Hence, genetic approaches and pharmaco-therapeutics to enhance mechanisms that maintain epigenome stability are prominent across all collaborative projects of this PPG and in this Project 2. During previous funding we uncovered chromatin alterations during mammalian senescence and aging, indeed we provided pioneering observations of altered histone acetylation during aging. Our results, with collaborative findings in this PPG, broadly support the concept of declining chromostasis during aging manifesting in epigenome dysregulation, with dire functional consequences. Our recent observations include (1) acquisition of new strong regulatory enhancers (“super-enhancers”) and hyper-connected enhancer “cliques” driving genes of senescence; (2) enhancer-to-promoter conversion within gene introns leading to “cryptic” transcriptional initiation; (3) evidence that metabolic pathways intersect with epigenetic pathways. To uncover the mechanisms and physiological importance of these new chromatin regulators and pathways in aging, we will carry out the following aims. In Aim 1, we will investigate how enhancers are rewired during senescence and aging with a focus on large enhancer communities or cliques. We will decipher how cliques are formed and identify major transcription factors that drive their formation. In Aim 2, we will investigate how cryptic transcription is initiated within genes, and transcription factors and epigenetic enzymes that regulate this process in senescence and aging. Further, our data suggest a link between cryptic initiation and cliques, to be investigated in detail. In Aim 3 we focus on a nuclear metabolic enzyme, PHDX, that interacts with the histone acetyltransferase KAT7 to activate senescence-associated secretory phenotypes. Overall, the proposed collaborative research will reveal chromatin mechanisms—connecting to metabolic mechanisms— underlying stability of the epigenome in longevity, with the potential to discover new therapeutic targets to intervene in age-related diseases and to extend healthy lifespan.

title: Targeting druggable coronavirus proteins
text: Coronaviruses, including SARS-CoV-2, pose obvious and imminent dangers to public health. This CAMPP proposal develops compounds that target multiple coronaviruses proteins and replication processes. These proteins include well established drug targets such as protease (Project 1) and replicase (Project 2), and as well as higher risk targets (Project 4). Project 3 – Targeting Druggable Coronavirus Proteins focuses on four less established viral processes that nonetheless have been successfully targeted in at least one proof-of-principle example. These include the coronaviral helicase nsp13 (Aim 1, led by Sumit Chandra at Scripps Research), the nucleocapsid (N) protein, which packages the RNA genome and associates with the budding virion (Aim 2, led by Suganya Selvarajah at Prosetta), the E protein, which encodes an ion channel whose activity likely contributes to virion assembly (Aim 3, led by John Guatelli from UCSD), and the spike (S) protein with mediates fusion of the viral and cellular membranes (Aim 4, lead by Michael Farzan at Scripps Florida). These four targets afford four parallel “shots on goal”. In each case, the lead laboratory has identified novel proof-of-principle chemical matter inhibiting the activity of each protein. These compounds are developed through a common pipeline, and in parallel each aim pursues a custom high-throughput screen designed to address the challenges unique to each target. In the later years of the proposal developmental resources are allocated to the most promising compounds. The overall structure of this proposal is thus designed to maximize the chance of developing an effective inhibitor or coronavirus replication.

title: Examination of the Dose Response Relationship Between Physical Activity and Arthritis-Attributable Outcomes
text:
This project aims to examine the effect of 3 durations of moderate to vigorous intensity physical activity
(45 min/week, 90 min/week, and 150 min/week) on arthritis-attributable outcomes in adults with arthritis as well
was explore whether these doses have differential effects on momentary symptoms. These results will provide
insight on whether engaging in activity below physical activity guidelines has beneficial effects on arthritis-
related outcomes.

title: Effects of the oral microbiome on Adverse Outcomes of Pediatric Hematopoietic Cell Transplantation
text:
This exploratory study will investigate the interkingdom interactions of the pediatric oral supergingival plaque
microbiome and its effect on comorbidity of hematopoetic cell transplant. Shotgun metagenomic sequencing
will be done to compare oral bacteria, archaea, fungi and viruses before and after transplant to identify
functional modules/networks in the oral microbiome that differentiate caries risk and markers of blood infection
in pediatric HCT recipients.

title: Advancing Acceptability and Ethical Readiness for Innovative HIV Cell and Gene Therapies in the United States
text:
8. PROJECT NARRATIVE
 Cell and gene therapy (CGT), aimed at making cells resistant to HIV or enhancing immune responses, is a
leading candidate for a scalable HIV cure with transformative potential for public health. This project will address
key U.S.-specific challenges by assessing the acceptability of HIV CGT among people with HIV (PWH), exploring
the experiences of trial participants and staff, and evaluating the feasibility of novel in vivo CGT research within
an end-of-life translational model. Findings will inform ethical trial design and policy, accelerating HIV cure
research and advancing healthcare innovation that will ultimately benefit the health of all Americans.

title: Decoding cellular history in longitudinally inaccessible tissues
text:
This research addresses a significant challenge in understanding human disease progression:
decoding cellular history in tissues that cannot be longitudinally sampled, such as the brain to
study Alzheimer's disease or the heart to study cardiomyopathy. This work will uncover the
hidden histories of cells beyond the observable tissue by developing innovative statistical and
artificial intelligence methods for single-cell sequencing leveraging lineage tracing, cohort-level
analyses, or paired multi-omics data. These advancements will improve our understanding of
complex biological processes, identify early disease markers, and open new pathways for
targeted interventions, ultimately enhancing public health and advancing biomedical science.

title: Elucidating resistance mechanisms and enhancing response to immune checkpoint blockade in central nervous system metastases from breast cancer
text:
In this grant, we propose to identify biomarkers of response and resistance to immunotherapy and potentially
new therapeutic targets for patients with brain metastases from breast cancer. Our application is relevant to the
public health because there are limited effective systemic therapies for patients with brain metastases. Relevant
to the NIH mission, the overarching objective of this study is to identify genetic alterations that are associated
with progression in patients with brain metastases receiving immunotherapy, and to explore novel combination
therapies, with the goal to identify optimal therapeutic approaches for this common neoplasm.

title: Quantitative Modeling of Protein-Nucleic Acid Binding
text:
Title: Quantitative Modeling of Protein–Nucleic Acid Binding
PI: Rohs, Remo
PROJECT NARRATIVE
Understanding how proteins interact with DNA and RNA is essential for deciphering gene regulation and
developing new treatments for disease. This project will create advanced AI-driven tools to model and predict
protein–nucleic acid interactions, enabling the rational design of gene-targeted therapies. The resulting
technologies will support precision medicine by enhancing our ability to decipher gene expression and molecular
interactions at the structural level.

title: Modeling the mucosal glycopeptide mesh for improved disease understanding and mucin-inspired biomaterial design
text:
Improved computational models of high-glycosylation proteins that capture their molecular
structure-dynamics are imperative to acquire detailed understanding of these critical biomedical
entities. We will use a combination of biophysics-based and machine learning driven approaches
to build predictive models of glycoproteins, using mucins as our study case. These models will be
harnessed to elucidate the molecular underpinnings that drive their function in normal and
diseased conditions, allowing for better therapeutic strategies, as well as aid in designing novel
mucin-mimetic biomaterials.

title: The Role of TRPV4 in Right Ventricular Cardiomyocyte Ca2+ Dysregulation in Pulmonary Hypertension
text:
Incidence and prevalence of pulmonary hypertension is rising worldwide and leads to pressure overload of the
right ventricle and progressive right heart dysfunction. Function of the Transient Potential Vanilloid 4 (TRPV4)
cation channel is upregulated in pressure-overloaded left ventricular cardiomyocytes, but the role of TRPV4 in
right-ventricular physiology is presently unknown. This proposal will study a novel link between Angiotensin II,
TRPV4, and ventricular performance and arrhythmia in the setting of pulmonary hypertension.

title: Maternal mediators of fetal growth restriction linked to prenatal alcohol exposure
text:
Prenatal Alcohol Exposure (PAE) is a common cause of fetal growth restriction, which is a
known risk factor for brain disability. The proposed studies meet a significant need for
mechanism-centered diagnostics and interventions for this important pregnancy complication
due to PAE and other etiologies. The goals of these studies are consistent with the goals outlined
in the 2017-2021 strategic plan of the National Institute of Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism
(NIAAA), to diagnose and to treat the consequences of alcohol use and misuse, including Fetal
Alcohol Spectrum Disorders (FASD).

title: Role of Programmed Cell Death Pathways in Bacterial Keratitis
text:
CDC reported that among the US population 34.2 million people of all ages—or 10.5% of the US population—
had diabetes in 2018. Diabetic patients are known to have a higher incidence of infection, including microbial
keratitis, with increased disease severity and higher rate of multi-drug resistance. The causes for increased
susceptibility and rapid progression of microbial keratitis at cellular and tissue levels are elusive. Using
Pseudomonas aeruginosa keratitis model of normal and diabetic mice in combination with RNA-seq and
sophisticated bioinformatic, we propose to investigate biological processes that contribute to the defects in
immune response and to identify means that reverse these adverse effects in diabetic corneas. CDC recently
reported one death, three with permanent vision loss, and 55 people infected with antibiotic-resistant P.
aeruginosa, linked to the use of EzriCare eye drops. Our proposed study is timely, clinically relevant, and will fill
a major knowledge gap and lead to better treatment for infectious keratitis for the patients with or without
diabetes.
